Comment 3.5: Fourth, from a methodological standpoint, the fabrication details are explicit, and the basic experimental arrangement is standard for photothermal measurements. The data on waveguide characterization, group index determination, and photothermal signal scaling with pump power all suggest competent execution. Nevertheless, the manuscript does not sufficiently highlight how these technical steps move beyond work already available in the literature on integrated photonic crystal sensors.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. In this work, we present a fundamentally new scheme of dual slow-light enhanced PTS with detailed theoretical formulation and experimental investigations. Therefore, our methodology aims to optimize the performance of the dual slow-light enhanced PTS, which has not been reported in previous literatures. Following your comment, we have updated the Discussion of the revised manuscript to highlight the advantages of our work clearly.
(1) We report a new theoretical framework as a guideline for PhCW design. Our perturbation theory on guided modes, along with the approximate solution of the heat transfer, provides a quantitative relationship between the dual slow-light PTS and the PhCW structures, such as the material properties, dimensions, and the suspended design. We also provide numerical simulations on a 3D Multiphysics model for separately analyze the optical and thermal dynamics. We include a detailed oscillation phenomenon analysis that explains how the group index influences the behavior of slow-light effect, particularly in the context of photothermal, thermo-optic, and interference effects. The PhCW optimization dramatically affects the pump absorption and probe photothermal effect, hence decides the dual slow-light PTS performance.
(2) We report the first experimental verification that the on-chip PTS sensitivity (i.e., photothermal efficiency) is proportional to the product of and , which is highly consistent with our theoretical formulation. Through photothermal characterization experiments, we detailed how this relationship is observed experimentally, emphasizing the linear scaling of the photothermal signal with the combined and across multiple device designs. This approach introduces a new method of quantifying and harnessing dual slow-light enhancement for gas sensing and other light-matter interactions.
Comment 3.6: Overall, the article offers an incremental contribution that confirms some expected advantages of dual slow-light enhancement in a photonic crystal waveguide. However, the claimed improvements do not convincingly surpass what other research groupshave demonstrated, nor does the manuscript provide a strong argument for a fundamentally new approach. Consequently, although the work is carefully executed, it does not appear to meet the high novelty and impact standards expected by a top-tier journal. In light of these considerations, the recommendation is to reject the paper. The demonstrated device achieves moderate performance gains that do not clearly outpace existing sensor architectures, and the authors’ discussion does not sufficiently establish the broader significance of these findings for integrated photonic gas sensing.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s constructive comment. We have updated the Discussion of the revised manuscript to highlight the advantages of our work clearly.
(1) In this work, we present a fundamentally new scheme of dual slow-light effect for the first time, and perform the first dual slow-light-based sensing enhancement with detailed theoretical formulation and experimental investigations.
(2) We present the first realization of dual slow-light enhanced on-chip PTS, which has not been reported for waveguide, for fiber and for free space. Our results demonstrate that the photothermal efficiency is proportional to the product of group indices of the pump and probe, which simultaneously enhances both the pump absorption and the probe phase modulation in a dispersion-engineered PhCW. This dual slow-light scheme amplifies the photothermal efficiency to 3.6×10⁻⁴ rad·cm·ppm⁻¹·mW⁻¹·m⁻¹, which surpass traditional free-space/fiber sensors by more than 3 orders of magnitude, and is over an order of magnitude higher than that of reported waveguide sensors.
(3) With a 1-mm-long sensing PhCW incorporated in a stabilized on-chip MZI with a footprint of 0.6 mm2, we demonstrate C H detection with a NEA·L sensitivity of 9.2×10⁻⁷, which surpasses previously reported waveguide gas sensors by 1-3 orders of magnitude. This sensor even approaches that of the most advanced free-space/fiber sensors, while offering distinct benefits in terms of compactness, CMOS compatibility, and scalable integration, which are key features for next-gen, miniaturized, and distributed gas sensing platforms.
(4) We demonstrate a compactintegration of a sensing device with suspended PhCW, on-chip MZI, and gas chamber. Such a miniaturization and integration level are not achievable with traditional fiber and waveguide systems, positioning our platform for future chip-scale sensing systems that could integrate light source and detector on a single chip.
(5) The demonstrated novel dual slow-light scheme is not limited to gas sensing. It is extendable to a broad range of photonic platforms, including liquid analyte detection, mid-IR integrated sensors, and other dual-light systems for studying light-matter interactions. The potential applications of this work span areas such as smart homes, point-of-care diagnostics, environmental monitoring, and wearable devices, etc.
